newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists would welcome euro-dollar parity.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists would welcome euro-dollar parity.

text.p: French Socialist party spokesman Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Friday that a one-for-one parity between the dollar and the euro would be a good thing from an economic point of view.

Speaking on the day the opposition Socialist party unveiled its manifesto for a two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, he also said the euro must be launched with Italy and Spain on January 1, 1999.
He noted it was up to financial markets to determine the exchange rate between the dollar and the new euro.
"From a strictly economic point of view, I think a parity of one-for-one is a good parity," he told Reuters.

That would imply a devaluation when compared to the current exchange rate for the European currency unit of 1.13 Ecus per dollar. The Ecu will be exchangeable for the euro on a one-for-one basis on January 1, 1999.

Asked about the cost of the Socialist party economic programme, which includes a pledge to create 700,000 jobs, he said, "None. There will be a redistribution of spending which is already there but which is inefficient. There will be no increase in public spending."

He added that France must continue to reduce its budget deficit, but said it should hold talks with its EU partners if its deficit was marginally over the ceiling set by the Maastricht treaty of three percent of gross domestic product.

"We have to do everything so that the budget deficit is as low as possible. If that produces 3.1 percent, it will produce 3.1 percent. The debate will then be a political debate with our partners but not the debate of accountants," he said.
He said a European growth pact sought by the Socialist party, which would include a new programme of public works, could add two percentage points to European gross domestic product.
Asked about how these public works would be financed, he said Europe "could use central bank reserves to guarantee borrowing after the launch of the euro".

"Central bank reserves are proportional to imports. Given that once we have the euro, there will no longer be internal balances of payments, there will obviously be credit lines available, not for spending, but at least to use as a guarantee," he said.
He also said that the Socialist party did not rule out using a law which would allow it to sell a small part of state-owned companies.
The party has said it is opposed to new state sales, including that of France Telecom, which the centre-right has slated for partial privatisation in June.
